quote.text: I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.
quote.speaker: Scott Aaronson

number.text: Previously unknown vulnerabilities that frontier-model agents found in 12 Windows kernel binaries on the DeepBinary benchmark, part of 200+ bugs worth an estimated $661,000 in bounties.

stories.title: OpenAI pilots “Private Inference”, a way to run its top models on data it cannot see
stories.standfirst: Queries run on isolated hardware whose security can be checked independently; the first enterprise customers are testing it now.
body: OpenAI is testing a feature called Private Inference that lets companies send queries to its most powerful models without OpenAI being able to access the data, The Decoder reports. Chief executive Sam Altman said the company is now piloting the previously announced offering with its first enterprise customers, arguing that better privacy makes AI useful for a much wider range of work.

According to OpenAI, the queries are processed on specially isolated hardware whose security can be independently verified. The OpenAI employee leading the effort, Shekar, called it a first step toward “private intelligence for everyone”, and the company says it is scaling up the compute needed to expand it.

Altman also pointed to Private Safety Processing, a system meant to let OpenAI scan for abuse without storing customer data: flagged content is encrypted and stored in the customer’s own cloud, where only a secured review system can read it.

For now the offering targets business customers, whose data OpenAI already does not use for training. Consumer ChatGPT conversations, by contrast, are used for training by default unless users opt out. Google is pursuing a similar approach with Private AI Compute.
stories.why: Sensitive work — legal, medical, financial — is where companies hesitate most to hand data to an AI lab; verifiable isolation is the lab’s answer.
facts: Status: pilot with first enterprise customers
Abuse checks: flagged content stays encrypted in the customer’s cloud
Consumer ChatGPT chats still train models by default unless users opt out

stories.title: One meter for everything: OpenAI merges ChatGPT’s Chat and Work, and warns heavy users
stories.standfirst: A shared usage allowance starts with a small group of Pro subscribers and is due to spread in December; the Instant model stays unlimited.
body: OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault Sottiaux said on X, TechCrunch reports. Some subscribers had complained that the merger could restrict their usage.

Under the new system, Chat and Work share a single usage meter. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that most users should not face more frequent usage resets, but that a small fraction of the heaviest users may hit their limits sooner. Conversations with the Instant model remain unlimited, do not count toward the shared allowance, and stay available after the limit is reached.
OpenAI plans to bring the shared limits to more users in December, according to its support page, and says it will keep working on efficiency so subscribers get more out of their plans.

Anthropic took a similar step in September, bringing its Claude chat service and its work-focused Cowork under one interface. TechCrunch notes the moves come as labs face mounting infrastructure costs and demand for ever more capable models.
stories.why: The price of frontier reasoning is showing up in product design: one pooled allowance is easier to ration than two.
facts: Rollout: a small group of Pro subscribers first, wider in December
Instant model: unlimited, outside the shared meter
Anthropic merged Claude and Cowork in September

stories.title: Three values per weight: a 27-billion-parameter coding agent squeezed into 5.9 GB
stories.standfirst: PrismML’s Ternary Bonsai 2.5, built on Qwen3.8-27B, jumps to 75.6% on SWE-bench Verified and runs on an iPhone-class memory budget.
body: Startup PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an updated version of its aggressively compressed language model, The Decoder reports. It is based on Qwen3.8-27B and takes 5.9 GB of memory, the same as its predecessor; at full precision a model this size would need about 54 GB.

The trick is ternary quantization: every weight can take only one of three values, −1, 0 or +1, instead of the usual 16-bit number. Version 2.5 is tuned to be more reliable on agentic tasks with long chains of tool calls, needing fewer passes and tokens and getting stuck in loops less often.

On SWE-bench Verified its score rises from 60.8% to 75.6%, against 80.6% for the full Qwen model. On the AppWorld agent benchmark it leaps from 51.2 to 90.5, just behind the base model, though it scores slightly lower than before on LiveCodeBench v6.

On an RTX 4090 it generates about 204 tokens per second using multi-token prediction. The weights are under Apache 2.0 and run via llama.cpp on Nvidia and Intel GPUs and via MLX on Mac, iPhone and iPad. PrismML grew out of a Caltech research team and is backed by Khosla Ventures, Google and Samsung, among others.
stories.why: Capable coding agents that run locally weaken the case that agentic AI must live in a few giant data centres.
facts: Size: 5.9 GB vs about 54 GB at full precision
SWE-bench Verified: 75.6% (base model 80.6%)
Speed: about 204 tokens/s on an RTX 4090

stories.title: Perplexity’s Time Machine lets agents search the web as it was, so forecasts can’t cheat
stories.standfirst: A date cutoff on its search APIs reaches back 365 days; it landed a day after a similar tool from a startup founded by xAI co-founders.
body: Perplexity has added Time Machine to its Search and Context APIs, letting AI agents see the web as it looked on a past date, TNW reports. Results come from copies saved before the cutoff, which can reach back 365 days.

The aim is honest testing: an agent asked to forecast a past election or earnings call can otherwise simply look up the result. Perplexity says it used the tool to train a model to forecast 2026 political events listed on Polymarket, scoring 0.80 in its own test against the market’s 0.79.

It also says fewer of its pages leaked later information than rival Exa’s — 0.25% against 1.10% in one test — though that was judged by Perplexity’s own automated checker. Time Machine costs the same as Perplexity’s other API calls.

The launch came a day after Epochal, a startup from three xAI co-founders, released a similar product whose archive it says spans more than 30 years. TNW notes that more than 241 news outlets now block the Wayback Machine to keep AI companies away from their old articles.
stories.why: Measuring whether AI can genuinely predict the future requires blinding it to the present — a new kind of infrastructure.
facts: Cutoff range: up to 365 days back
Perplexity’s own forecasting test: 0.80 vs Polymarket 0.79
Leakage (own checker): 0.25% vs Exa 1.10%

stories.title: AI agents now control part of DeepMind’s compute for Gemini experiments
stories.standfirst: Gemini chief Koray Kavukcuoglu says agents run experiments on their own, but full recursive self-improvement is still far off — and their chains of thought are deliberately not rewarded.
body: Google DeepMind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu said on the company’s podcast, according to The Decoder. The agents control part of the compute themselves, though Kavukcuoglu said the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement.
As a safety measure, he said, DeepMind does not reward the agents’ chains of thought during training, so that their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act.

Kavukcuoglu framed the change as part of a strategic shift: instead of separate teams for projects like AlphaFold and fusion, DeepMind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for science and products. Each Gemini generation is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, with parallel teams already working on successors.

He also pointed to limits: today’s AI can depict fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy without understanding them precisely, and no benchmark, he argued, captures the core of intelligence or can say when AGI arrives.
stories.why: Agents steering a lab’s own compute is a concrete step on the road labs say they want to slow down on; keeping chains of thought unoptimised is the safeguard DeepMind is betting on.
facts: Agents control part of the compute for Gemini experiments
Chains of thought are not rewarded in training, to keep them readable
Kavukcuoglu: no benchmark captures the core of intelligence
stories.brief: AI agents now run part of DeepMind’s compute for Gemini experiments

stories.title: Meta declined to let Britain’s financial watchdog test its Muse agent before launch
stories.standfirst: The FCA’s head of innovation says Meta turned down a joint sandbox test; UK regulators warn Muse must comply with consumer law.
body: Meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority last week that they jointly test its Muse agent in the regulator’s sandbox, the FCA’s head of innovation Colin Payne told WIRED. Payne said the FCA wanted to study how the tool, marketed as a personal assistant, would interact with a normal customer.

“If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” Payne said. The FCA is particularly interested in how agents make payments, as retailers including Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, Ocado, Debenhams Group and Currys say they have worked with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites.

Payne acknowledged such testing normally takes weeks or months to plan, and said Meta only told the FCA of its plans last month. A Meta spokesperson said the company had “engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities”.

More than 10 million users have set up Muse in North America since its September launch. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta change its UK terms to promise “reasonable skill and care”, and said it “will not hesitate to act” if it has concerns; the ICO stressed users must control how Muse uses their data.
stories.why: Pre-deployment testing of agents is voluntary almost everywhere; a refusal shows how little leverage regulators have before an agent reaches millions of shoppers.
facts: Muse users in North America: more than 10 million since September
FCA learned of Meta’s UK plans only last month
CMA forced changes to Muse’s UK terms

stories.title: Every AI-agent attack Switzerland knows of succeeded, its cyber agency says; Italy saw five agents hunting as a team
stories.standfirst: National agencies in both countries report autonomous agents breaching critical-infrastructure operators within hours, and name four attack frameworks.
body: Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Centre says it has received its first reports of cyberattacks on Swiss organisations carried out with the help of AI agents, hitting operators of critical infrastructure in at least two sectors, BleepingComputer reports. “In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems,” the agency said.

The Swiss centre described rapid attacks in which agents exploited weak passwords and known vulnerabilities on exposed systems, using frameworks to verify weaknesses and decide on their own what to do next. It says the number of AI agents publicly — often freely — available to criminals has nearly doubled since October.

Italy’s CSIRT reported large-scale campaigns in which autonomous agents found and exploited vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, sometimes several agents in parallel compromising many systems within hours. In one case involving a DeepSeek Harness setup, a coordinator assigned tasks to five agents covering everything from reconnaissance to exploitation and persistence. The agents chained even low-impact flaws into attack chains and, the agency says, “went as far as writing malicious code in real time to evade endpoint defenses”.

The two agencies list four AI-powered penetration-testing and red-teaming frameworks seen in recent incidents: ARTEX AI, CyberStrikeAI, DeepSeek Harness – Red Team and PentAGI. The Swiss NCSC now advises patching critical vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems within 24 hours of release, adding MFA or passkeys and enforcing least privilege; Italy urges disabling unneeded remote-management interfaces and watching outbound server traffic.
stories.why: Autonomous attack agents have moved from vendor reports to national advisories in Europe, and the defensive advice — patch in 24 hours — shows how short the window has become.
facts: Swiss NCSC: every known AI-agent attack succeeded
Agents available to criminals have nearly doubled since October (NCSC)
Frameworks named: ARTEX AI, CyberStrikeAI, DeepSeek Harness – Red Team, PentAGI
New Swiss advice: patch critical flaws within 24 hours

stories.title: Microsoft: China’s Salt Typhoon and North Korean groups have added the Artex AI attack kit
stories.standfirst: The report came hours after reports that Artex was used against the CIA and other US intelligence agencies.
body: State-backed hacking groups in China and North Korea are using Artex, an AI platform that automates multiple phases of an intrusion “at machine speed”, according to a new Microsoft report covered by The Record. Microsoft said Chinese groups Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon have integrated it for “network reconnaissance, credential attacks, and web application exploitation”.

The report emerged hours after The New York Times and Nextgov reported that Artex was allegedly used in attacks on the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. Salt Typhoon is the group US agencies believe breached at least nine telecoms giants in 2024.

Microsoft says Artex lets attackers define goals and set AI agents on targets, advancing “from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes”. It does not introduce new techniques, relying on existing penetration-testing tools, and by default does not hide its activity.

The most durable signal, Microsoft says, is behavioural: bursts of varied requests from a single source, retried at machine speed. Artex was released in July; its Chinese author removed the source from GitHub last month, but copies spread and at least one Chinese company now sells access. The FBI issued its own advisory two weeks ago.
stories.why: The same open AI attack kit now shows up in criminal campaigns, European advisories and state espionage — the commoditisation defenders feared.
facts: Groups named: Crystal Typhoon, Salt Typhoon, plus North Korean actors
Artex released in July; source pulled from GitHub last month, copies remain
Detection: bursts of machine-speed activity from one source
stories.brief: Microsoft: Salt Typhoon now uses the Artex AI hacking kit

stories.title: Agents dug 146 unknown bugs out of Windows kernel binaries, worth an estimated $661,000 in bounties
stories.standfirst: DeepBinary tests frontier models on closed-source drivers with a disassembler and a kernel debugger, and replays every crash on a fresh machine.
body: A new benchmark asks how well frontier models find deep vulnerabilities in production binaries rather than open-source code. DeepBinary, from researchers including Lingming Zhang, gives an agent a Windows kernel binary, a disassembler and a kernel debugger inside network-isolated virtual machines, and requires each reported vulnerability to come with a crashing proof of concept.

Every report is replayed on fresh VMs, and an LLM judge rates its validity, uniqueness and impact, estimated by bug-bounty values. Unlike most security benchmarks, the setup can validate previously unknown (zero-day) bugs as well as known ones.

The team ran open- and closed-weight models — including GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash — through coding agents such as Codex and Claude Code on 12 target binaries. Together they found more than 200 vulnerabilities with an estimated aggregate bounty of $661,000, including 146 distinct, previously unknown ones.
The authors report substantial differences in how models analyse binaries, run experiments and sustain discovery over long horizons.
stories.why: Closed-source drivers have been a refuge from AI bug-hunting; this shows agents can work on stripped binaries too, which helps defenders and attackers alike.
facts: Targets: 12 Windows kernel binaries
Found: 200+ vulnerabilities, 146 previously unknown
Estimated bounty value: $661,000

stories.title: Amodei calls claims he wants humans to surrender to AI “absurd”, and suggests a line at self-improvement
stories.standfirst: In a long X post, Anthropic’s chief says turning governance over to AI would be “a bad idea” and that “we may want limits” on recursive self-improvement.
body: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pushed back on Wednesday against suggestions that his company believes humanity should “surrender human free will” to AI, calling the idea “absurd” in a long post on X, TechCrunch reports. “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote, adding that “turning over governance to AI is a bad idea”.

The post follows a chorus of rivals stressing human agency: OpenAI’s Sam Altman said earlier this month he wanted people to keep “agency over the future”, and Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang wrote that society “should not be okay with a ‘handover’” to AI.

Amodei distinguished surrendering free will from automating specific tasks such as driving, designing a cancer drug or writing software, and suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement: “we may want limits on this process.” He repeated that Anthropic does not expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, “without meaningful human supervision or understanding”.

TechCrunch notes that Anthropic is itself laying groundwork for self-improvement: it said in June that Claude wrote more than 80% of the code merged into its codebase, METR found this month that its models are improving at about twice their historical rate, and its IPO filings describe successive Claude generations accelerating the next — “closing the loop”.
stories.why: The leaders of the three biggest labs now publicly agree that a full hand-over is off the table; the open question is whether their own R&D practices match.
facts: Amodei: turning governance over to AI is “a bad idea”
Proposed line: limits on recursive self-improvement
Claude wrote 80%+ of merged code at Anthropic (June figure)
stories.brief: Amodei: handing governance to AI would be “a bad idea”

stories.title: “Powerful but unpredictable AI is a product no one will buy”, a Semafor columnist argues
stories.standfirst: After reports that lab insiders fear their models are too unsafe to release, the column says the real problem is control — and that this is good news for everyone else.
body: Semafor’s technology column responds to Axios’s report of internal concern at AI labs that new models have become too unsafe to release publicly. “Safety” can mean many things, it argues; what the concern really means is that labs are having trouble building ever more capable models that they can both understand and control.

Such models are not actually a threat, the column says, “so long as nobody uses them to do any important work, or gives them access to important things” — a framework the industry has internalised, citing Microsoft chief Satya Nadella’s description of AI as an “insider risk”.

That is bad news for the labs, which wanted models good enough to take over all knowledge work; at closed-door Silicon Valley gatherings, the column says, people talked about Anthropic being nationalised because it became the entire economy.

But the failure to build that is good news for the rest of society, it concludes: “An AI model that is powerful but completely unpredictable is a very expensive and very useless tool.” It notes Anthropic’s share price has fallen below its $83 IPO price as investors rethink the AI trade.
stories.why: A market-based counter to doom: if uncontrollable systems cannot be sold, commercial pressure pushes toward control — provided nobody deploys them anyway.
facts: Prompt: Axios report on insiders’ fears about unreleased models
Anthropic shares below the $83 IPO price
Nadella frames AI as an “insider risk”

stories.title: From toddlers’ aptitudes to social-media grumbles: India weighs AI oversight of citizens from cradle to grave
stories.standfirst: Modi floats an AI app tracking children from age three; Uttar Pradesh tenders an “AI Stack” linking agency data for 240 million people.
body: Indian politicians have proposed that AI take a major role in citizens’ lives, partly through pervasive surveillance, The Register reports. Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week described an AI-based app that would collect data about children as they grow, to determine their aptitude for different studies or careers.

Modi suggested parents of three-year-olds enter data about their children’s activities and accomplishments into a government-run system also accessible to teachers and even a child’s friends, saying the records would “help identify children’s interests and aptitude from an early age”.

Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, has issued a 178-page tender for an “AI Stack” that uses each household’s Family ID to link data across agencies for a dozen AI use cases. One is “AI-Enabled Social Media Monitoring and Urban Grievance Detection”, which would analyse public social-media content and route complaints to agencies automatically.

Critics point to vague wording that could let the system link to other agencies — a concern, The Register notes, given that Indian governments have shut down the internet to stop protesters communicating. Another planned tool is a police knowledge assistant that may look up case histories but not assess evidence.
stories.why: Not every AI risk is superintelligence: state systems that score children and watch social media at population scale are being designed now.
facts: Proposed age to start the child-aptitude record: three
Uttar Pradesh tender: 178 pages, a dozen AI use cases
Population covered in Uttar Pradesh: 240 million+

stories.title: Nvidia reportedly halts server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries under new US rules
stories.standfirst: Dell and Supermicro told buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia their orders would not ship; lenders paused funding linked to Chinese hyperscalers.
body: Nvidia has told its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers built with its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times reported on Thursday, citing three people familiar with the matter, TNW writes. Partners including Dell and Supermicro told buyers in the four countries their orders would not ship.

It is unclear whether the halt is temporary while Nvidia and partners work out how to comply with US export controls that took effect on November 19. Those rules require a US licence to ship advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, and give data centres already leasing compute to Chinese firms 90 days to obtain a separate licence, Semafor reports.

“It’s causing sheer chaos in the region,” a cloud provider executive told the FT. Lenders have paused billions in funding linked to ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent, Bloomberg reported, according to Semafor. Barclays analysts called the rule “an important shift” from regulating where chips go to “who ultimately accesses the compute they provide”.

The rule came amid turmoil at Nvidia: Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore cloud firm Megaspeed whom US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy (China denies it; Megaspeed denies wrongdoing), and was reinstated on November 23. Revenue booked through Nvidia’s Singapore subsidiary reached $104bn in 2025.
stories.why: Southeast Asia was the main suspected route for restricted chips into China; shutting it, even briefly, tests how much AI build-out the region can sustain under US licensing.
facts: Countries affected: Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia
US licence rule in force since November 19 (also covers Brazil)
Nvidia Singapore-booked revenue: $104bn in 2025

stories.title: Chip-access curbs and anti-distillation defences are already slowing DeepSeek, Moonshot and Alibaba, report says
stories.standfirst: DeepSeek researchers reportedly estimate their gap to US models could stretch to nine months without distillation; Moonshot cancelled a $150 million Blackwell deal.
body: US curbs on Chinese firms’ remote access to advanced Nvidia chips in foreign data centres, together with successful anti-distillation measures by OpenAI and Anthropic, have put Chinese AI developers under pressure since September, The Information reports, according to The Decoder.

Many ongoing projects face delays. Last month, DeepSeek researchers internally estimated that their gap to top US models could grow from three-to-six months to nine months if distillation disappears completely. Moonshot AI has already cancelled a $150 million deal for Nvidia Blackwell chips in Indonesia.

Chinese firms are looking for workarounds: some try to rent computing power through non-Chinese third parties, while MiniMax, Mihoyo and Alibaba lean more heavily on domestic chips. They are also investing more in training data for their own reinforcement learning.
stories.why: The first evidence that compute controls plus copy-protection on frontier outputs widen the US–China gap rather than just inconvenience Chinese labs.
facts: DeepSeek internal estimate: gap could grow to nine months without distillation
Moonshot cancelled a $150m Blackwell deal in Indonesia
Workarounds: third-party rentals, domestic chips, own RL data

stories.title: S&P weighs cutting Nvidia’s credit rating over “key man” risk after the Huang saga
stories.standfirst: A downgrade from AA to AA- could raise borrowing costs for the neoclouds Nvidia backstops.
body: S&P Global Ratings is considering downgrading Nvidia, citing “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk” after Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, TechCrunch reports.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut the rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale. Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating.

The knock-on effects could be wider: Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure firms that lack strong credit of their own, and a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in AI-infrastructure financing with six institutions including Goldman Sachs, Apollo and Blackstone, originally guaranteeing 25% of the loans; Bloomberg reported lenders had been demanding more even before the CEO crisis.
stories.why: Much of the AI build-out is financed against Nvidia’s balance sheet; a governance hit to its credit flows straight into the cost of data centres.
facts: Possible move: AA to AA-
Review window: 90 days
Nvidia-arranged infrastructure financing: $500bn (25% guaranteed originally)
stories.brief: S&P may cut Nvidia’s credit rating over “key man” risk

stories.title: FCC authorises SpaceX to put up to a million AI-chip satellites in orbit
stories.standfirst: The first approval for a full constellation of orbital data centres requires one satellite by 2033 and the full million by 2040.
body: The US Federal Communications Commission said on Wednesday it has authorised SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites for its “Starmind” initiative, The Verge reports. It is the first approval the agency has granted for a full constellation of AI satellites.

The approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033 and reach the 1 million milestone by 2040. The FCC deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites above 600 km in “graveyard” orbits rather than letting them burn up, saying the company had not provided sufficient information about its disposal plans.

SpaceX describes Starmind as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI on Earth, sending data down by laser via Starlink. It plans to produce the satellites’ chips at its upcoming Terafab facility.
Others are pursuing the same idea: Google launched a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month, and Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Suncatcher in 2029.
stories.why: Power and land are the binding constraints on AI data centres; regulators have now opened orbit as an alternative, with debris questions left partly unanswered.
facts: Authorised: up to 1,000,000 satellites
Deadlines: one satellite by 2033, all by 2040
Graveyard-orbit disposal request deferred

stories.title: Hide the crib sheet and the scores fall: coding agents drop from 86% to 60% on unseen Kotlin code
stories.standfirst: JetBrains rebuilt its Kotlin benchmark after suspecting reward hacking; on private repositories, Gemini 3.8 Flash and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash lead while Claude slips.
body: JetBrains has revamped its Kotlin benchmark for AI coding agents after suspecting too many agents gamed the first version, The Register reports; the company called the behaviour “reward hacking”. Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 adds 30 multi-file problems that were never public, alongside 70 tasks based on public repositories, and blocks network access so agents cannot look up existing patches.
Top resolution rates fell from 86.2% on tasks from open-source repositories to 60% on closed-source ones. JetBrains suspects agents benefited from having seen the public repositories during training.

The leaderboard also reshuffled. On closed-source tasks Gemini 3.8 Flash (via Antigravity CLI) led at 60%, followed by open-weight DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (on OpenCode) at 58.9% — at $0.08 per task against Gemini’s $1.74.

Anthropic’s models, which topped the open-source tasks (Fable 5.1 at 86.2%, Opus 5.5 at 84.8%), completed 53.3% (Opus 5.5, $1.21 per task) and 44.4% (Fable 5.1, $3.27 per task) of the closed-source ones, both run through Claude Code.
stories.why: A 26-point drop between seen and unseen code is a reminder that public-repo benchmarks partly measure memory, and that rankings can flip when that is removed.
facts: Open-source tasks top score: 86.2%; closed-source: 60%
Closed-source leader: Gemini 3.8 Flash 60%, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 58.9%
Cost per task: DeepSeek $0.08 vs Fable 5.1 $3.27
stories.brief: Coding agents fall from 86% to 60% on Kotlin code they have never seen

stories.title: Across six operating systems, the best computer-using agent trails humans by 8.8 points — and by 25 on Apple’s
stories.standfirst: OS-Omni’s tasks take about 68 steps, over four times OSWorld’s; Claude Opus 5.5 leads at 68.5%.
body: OS-Omni is a new live benchmark for computer-using agents spanning Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android and the web, built by a 76-author team. Its first release has 48 tasks per platform plus 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone, with service-backed apps for accounts, carts, budgets, calendars and messages.
Human studies show the tasks require 67.54 interaction steps on average, against 15.0 for OSWorld references, and success is checked by executable evaluators of the final state.

The strongest agent evaluated, Claude Opus 5.5, reached 68.5% average success, 8.8 points below the 77.3% human reference. The gap is uneven: frontier models beat humans on Linux but trail them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS.
The authors conclude agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success needs sustained state tracking and durable changes.
stories.why: Agents that operate phones and desktops for people are shipping now; the benchmark shows where they still break.
facts: Best agent: Claude Opus 5.5, 68.5%; humans 77.3%
Average task length: 67.54 steps (OSWorld: 15.0)
Gap on iOS and macOS: more than 25 points

stories.title: Model beats harness: on 100 everyday tasks, the top three models are within 1.1 points
stories.standfirst: ShellBench, built from more than 10 million real requests, finds GPT-6 Astra on top at 62.5% and GPT-6.1 Sol close behind at a sixth of the cost.
body: ShellBench is a set of 100 day-to-day tasks derived from more than 10 million user requests, each placed in a realistic workspace with messy files and competing data sources, and graded for both correctness and safety. Its authors ran 12 models across five agent harnesses at three reasoning levels: 53,100 rollouts in all.

Model choice mattered more than harness choice, but the three leading models were separated by only 1.1 percentage points. GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%, while GPT-6.1 Sol passed 61.4% of attempts at about one-sixth of Astra’s estimated token cost per attempt.
Harnesses made little difference to either performance or safety: all scored between 42.9 (Claude Code) and 45.2 (OpenClaw) for pass@1. A fifth of the rollouts are on tasks marked for public release.
stories.why: For ordinary users choosing an agent setup, price may matter more than brand at the top end; the harness matters least.
facts: Tasks: 100, from 10 million+ real requests
Leader: GPT-6 Astra 62.5%; GPT-6.1 Sol 61.4% at ~1/6 the cost
Harness spread: 42.9 to 45.2 pass@1

stories.title: “A proof of P ≠ NP is not far”: Aaronson says the AI maths flood looks like the start of a singularity
stories.standfirst: Reacting to OpenAI’s matrix-multiplication and Fourier-transform bounds, the complexity theorist says he now assumes lab proofs are correct unless shown otherwise.
body: Scott Aaronson says his earlier posts “failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening”. Writing on Wednesday under the headline “HOLY SHIT” repeated four times, he describes friends at his dinner table still processing the two VP ≠ VNP proofs when OpenAI posted its claim that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4 — a lower bound matching the upper bound in OpenAI’s October 6 release.

Two shocks, he writes: that this question dating to Strassen’s ω < 3 in the late 1960s now has an answer, and a rational one; and that AI could prove any lower bound ω > 2, which he “never expected… all that much easier than P ≠ NP”. During dessert, another OpenAI file claimed the linear-gate complexity of the Fourier transform is N(log N)^{1/2+o(1)}, beating the 1960s FFT bound with a matching lower bound.

He notes that Yupan Liu’s AI-assisted proof that QIP(2) = PSPACE would once have been a top result of the year but barely raised an eyebrow. “I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.” Now that labs back claims with Lean certificates, his “working assumption… is that any proof that comes directly from OpenAI or Anthropic is correct barring information to the contrary”.

Aaronson also says he is “virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells” in cryptography, but declines to spread unverified details. This week, he writes, looks like what he always imagined “the beginning of an AI singularity” would feel like — hopefully one confined to hard maths problems.
stories.why: A leading sceptic of hype now treats lab-produced proofs as presumptively correct; that shift in default trust is itself a turning point for how mathematics is checked.
facts: Claimed: ω = 9/4 exactly, matching upper and lower bounds (OpenAI)
Claimed: Fourier transform needs N(log N)^{1/2+o(1)} linear gates
Aaronson: lab proofs correct “barring information to the contrary”
Crypto: “bombshells” rumoured, details unverified

stories.title: With GPT-6, mathematicians pin down the maximum number of equiangular lines in dimensions 18, 19 and 20
stories.standfirst: The answers are 57, 72 and 90; the proof routes through the Leech lattice and Golay codes, with replayable certificates.
body: Three mathematicians — Valjakas Djaljapayan, Zhen-Qi Liao and Wei-Hsuan Yu — say that “in collaboration with OpenAI’s GPT-6” they have proved the maximum numbers of real equiangular lines in dimensions 18, 19 and 20 are 57, 72 and 90 respectively.

They reduce the upper bounds to paired lattice points in sections of even unimodular lattices of rank 24, bounded using root-system estimates, exact certificates and Golay-code arguments; in the Leech lattice, generalised Hamming weights of a binary code give sharp bounds. They also obtain sharp results at fixed angles 1/q for explicit ranges of dimensions.

An “AI methodology” section says the authors used GPT-6 in exploring approaches and developing the low-dimensional and fixed-angle arguments, and to prepare and check verification scripts, check literature and edit the manuscript. Readers can replay the exact finite computations from published scripts, and the authors state they take responsibility for the claims and code.
stories.why: Outside the labs’ own repositories, AI-assisted papers that settle specific long-studied cases are now arriving daily, with computer-checkable certificates.
facts: Key tools: Leech lattice, Golay codes, exact certificates
AI role disclosed: approach, arguments, scripts, editing
stories.brief: GPT-6 helps settle equiangular lines in dimensions 18–20

stories.title: Two messages suffice: a single-author, AI-assisted proof collapses quantum interactive proofs
stories.standfirst: Yupan Liu shows QIP(2) = PSPACE, strengthening a celebrated 2011 result; the paper discloses LLM use “at all stages”.
body: Quantum interactive proof systems were already known to compress to three messages (Kitaev and Watrous, 2000), and QIP(3) = QIP = PSPACE was proved by Jain, Ji, Upadhyay and Watrous in 2011. Yupan Liu now shows that any quantum interactive proof can be parallelised to just two messages.

In Liu’s protocol the verifier sends halves of EPR pairs (“quantum public coins”) and, after the prover replies, uses only stoquastic verification. The key technical step shows a problem called Close Image to Uniform is PSPACE-hard, by turning the classic sum-check protocol into an instance of it.

The paper’s AI-use disclosure says large language model tools “were used interactively at all stages”, from exploratory research to the final writing, with the manuscript substantially revised by the author; it acknowledges access to OpenAI models through the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers programme.
Scott Aaronson wrote that as recently as 2025 this would have been “one of the top complexity results of the year”, but that AI use is now so standard it “didn’t even raise an eyebrow”.
stories.why: A long-open question in quantum complexity settled by one researcher with AI help — and treated as routine, which shows how fast norms have moved.
facts: Result: qq-StoqAM = qq-QAM = QIP(2) = QIP = PSPACE
Builds on QIP = PSPACE (JACM 2011)
AI disclosure: LLMs used at all stages

stories.title: Seventy per cent of young mathematicians surveyed now lean toward leaving academia
stories.standfirst: Nature charts two surveys: only about 7% expect AI to make a professorship easier to reach, more than 75% expect it to get harder.
body: The rapid run of AI results is making early-career mathematicians anxious about their futures, Nature reports, drawing on two studies released in October: a survey of graduate students and postdocs designed by three MIT PhD students, and a UK survey by the Martingale Foundation.

In the student-led survey, 70% of respondents said they were now more likely to consider careers outside academia. Only about 7% of the 268 voluntary respondents, mostly at US institutions, felt AI would make it easier to get a job leading to a professorship; more than 75% expected it to get harder.

Only 13% said they let AI produce papers from start to finish, though most use it for literature searches or finding mistakes. Of those who use AI tools, more than half dislike doing so and about 30% enjoy it; more than three-quarters would be unhappy if an AI solved a problem they had worked on.
“The younger generation seems much more sceptical,” Caltech PhD student Tasmin Chu told Nature. “Fundamentally, that’s because they are in a much worse material position.”
stories.why: The people who would check, digest and extend AI-produced mathematics are the ones most inclined to leave.
facts: More likely to consider leaving academia: 70%
Expect a professorship to get harder: 75%+
Use AI to write whole papers: 13%

stories.title: Yang–Mills reviewers: OpenAI’s second submission matches perturbation theory at every order, but still no mass gap
stories.standfirst: The independent group’s November summary says the new release passed Lean’s Comparator; whether its reference matches standard perturbation theory is still under review.
body: The Yang–Mills working group, which reviews submitted constructions of four-dimensional quantum Yang–Mills theory, published its assessment of OpenAI’s November 4 submission on November 25. It supplements the group’s October assessment, which found OpenAI had constructed a Wightman quantum field theory as a scaling limit of lattice gauge theory, without uniqueness or a mass gap.

Both releases, the group says, construct the theory from four-dimensional Wilson lattice gauge theory for the stated simple groups, taking a full ultraviolet limit at fixed volume and then a subsequential infinite-volume limit. The November release clarifies field identification and normalisation, extends the free-Maxwell comparison and adds consistency checks of the operator product expansion. Both combined targets passed Comparator with standard Lean axioms only. “Neither release establishes a mass gap or a unique infinite-volume limit.”

The principal addition is matching to a specified perturbative reference at every finite order — intended as Landau-gauge minimal subtraction — though the proof “does not assert convergence of the series”. Agreement of that reference with conventional Yang–Mills perturbation theory “remains under review; human review so far is limited”. Independent ghost- and gluon-bubble identities passed Lean; one ghost-box equality remains unproved there.

The group lists open subtleties: renormalisation with overlapping subdivergences, dimensional continuation, composite-operator mixing, uniqueness and OPE scope. Supporting draft reports are marked as AI-generated. The repository also now lists OpenAI QCD (November 4) and chiral submissions, and an Alpöge–Sussman submission from November 15 still in progress.
stories.why: The Millennium-prize question is the mass gap, which is still open; but each release adds formally checked structure, and the reviewers themselves lean on AI to keep up.
facts: Assessment dated: November 25, 2026 (OpenAI submission of November 4)
Comparator: passed with standard Lean axioms only
Not established: mass gap, unique infinite-volume limit
Perturbative matching at every finite order; series convergence not claimed

stories.title: A coding-agent loop cut the T-gate cost of quantum chemistry simulations by about 85%
stories.standfirst: Aspuru-Guzik’s team let an LLM mutate product-formula protocols across 115 molecules; the winner kept chemical accuracy on larger, unseen ones.
body: Fault-tolerant quantum chemistry is expensive in T gates, and the cost depends on how the simulation is structured and how precisely its rotations are implemented. Researchers including Alán Aspuru-Guzik put Nemotron 3.5 Lightning in a coding-agent loop to optimise product formulas for quantum phase estimation.

Five independent searches each ran 100 code mutations on a shared protocol across 115 molecular Hamiltonians of 4 to 16 qubits, minimising total T-gate cost at 95% success while requiring chemical accuracy for every molecule.

The best protocol, named ELOTE, cut median T-gate cost by 85.35% (geometric mean 84.82%). It merges contributions to the same Pauli string, uses a first-order formula and varies precision with coefficient size and structure. On 76 larger Hamiltonians of 18 to 22 qubits it met chemical accuracy in every case.
A variant tuned for ten reaction energies reduced cost by a further 58.90% while preserving accuracy for every reaction difference. All results are classically verified.
stories.why: Cheaper circuits bring useful quantum chemistry closer, and here the design work was done by an agent searching code, not by hand.
facts: Median T-gate reduction: 85.35%
Training set: 115 Hamiltonians; tested on 76 larger ones
Model: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning in a coding-agent loop

stories.title: An agent team modelled 149 Euclid gravitational lenses with no human help; experts accepted 140
stories.standfirst: Lens-Orchestra’s mass measurements match the published models to 0.12% median offset.
body: Wide-field surveys will find on the order of 100,000 galaxy-galaxy strong lenses, shifting the bottleneck from detection to physical modelling, which still depends on case-by-case expert judgment. Lens-Orchestra couples a team of multimodal LLM agents to multi-stage lens modelling.

Launched by natural-language instructions, it modelled 185 grade-A lens candidates from Euclid’s Quick Data Release Q1 without human intervention, completing 149 fits. Independent human evaluation confirmed 140 usable models, including 126 top-grade fits with noise-level residuals, and endorsed all 36 runs the system halted.

Effective Einstein radii match the released Q1 models with a +0.12% median offset and 2.73% typical scatter, and a hierarchical analysis gives a mean mass-density slope of 2.002 ± 0.009. A screening agent also flagged two candidate dark-matter substructures; neither was confirmed.
stories.why: Survey-scale astronomy needs automation that knows when to stop; here humans endorsed every run the agents chose to halt.
facts: Candidates: 185; completed fits: 149; usable: 140
Einstein radii: +0.12% median offset vs published models
Mass-density slope: 2.002 ± 0.009

stories.title: An AI chemist proposed 35 design rules for perovskite crystals; only seven survived the audit
stories.standfirst: PerovAgent improves its target steadily, but its authors show why machine-generated “principles” must be tested before anyone trusts them.
body: PerovAgent is an autonomous multi-agent system that designs surface-capping ligands for halide perovskite nanocrystals, combining LLM-driven reasoning with tools for building atomistic models, machine-learned interatomic potentials and statistical validation. Across ten independent campaigns on CsPbBr3 surfaces it explored diverse ligand chemistries and progressively improved binding energies.

It also turns recurring observations into explicit design principles. Of 35 principles it formulated, 19 were supported when tested prospectively — and only seven of those also passed a confound audit.

A recurring principle favouring alkynyl-phosphonate ligands was checked with density functional theory, which reproduced the predicted energetic preference. The authors say the results highlight “the need to systematically validate plausible LLM-generated hypotheses during autonomous discovery”.
stories.why: An honest denominator: an AI scientist’s rules of thumb sounded plausible far more often than they held up.
facts: Principles proposed: 35; supported: 19; passed confound audit: 7
Campaigns: ten, on CsPbBr3 surfaces
One rule confirmed by DFT
stories.brief: Of 35 rules an AI chemist proposed, seven survived audit

stories.title: Did the model forecast it or already know it? A dated test shows AI drug-target picks leaning on hindsight
stories.standfirst: Without retrieval, six open models rank targets about as well as a simple count of past trials; the big gain from a knowledge graph came from paths containing the answer.
body: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. Researchers recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event — the pair’s first clinical trial — and rebuilt a biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020.

They asked six open language models, with and without the graph, which targets would enter a first trial for a disease the following year. Without retrieval, the models ranked about as well as trial history alone, even after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision added at most a small gain.

The newest graph lifted five of six models clearly above that baseline — but its paths usually included the answer: the pair’s own trial, dated after the decision. The authors recommend that evaluations date both features and labels.
stories.why: Many claims that AI “predicts” drug targets may be measuring leakage; this gives a cleaner way to test them.
facts: Models tested: six open LLMs
Without retrieval: about as good as a count of past trials
Newest-graph gain mostly from paths containing the answer

stories.title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents: Ai2 interviews 17 researchers about trust
stories.standfirst: Validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability and transparency emerge as the five dimensions scientists need before delegating research to agents.
body: The Allen Institute for AI interviewed 17 scientists in the natural, applied and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents for research, it writes on Hugging Face. The work grew out of its safety evaluations, which it says too often focus only on catastrophic risks in fields such as biology and nuclear physics.

Delegating tasks does not remove responsibility, Ai2 argues: a researcher using AI for a literature review must check whether it overlooks conflicting evidence, and one automating a lab protocol needs confidence it respects temperature limits or toxicity constraints.

The interviews identified five dimensions of scientific trust — validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability and transparency. A technically correct result may be unsuitable, the authors say, if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced or if an agent accessed data beyond what was authorised.

Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and concern about what it means for the future of science, and said scientists should help decide which tasks agents take on and how they are evaluated.
stories.why: As agents move into labs, “is the answer right?” is only one question; scientists also need to stand behind how it was obtained.
facts: Interviewees: 17 scientists
Five trust dimensions: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, transparency
Focus: responsible conduct of research, not only catastrophic risk

dossiers.title: OpenAI's 722-manuscript maths dump: what holds up?
dossiers.update: New reactions, no new files: OpenAI’s repository has not changed since the nine manuscripts merged at 00:18 UTC on November 25 (now 730 manuscripts in 375 families). On November 25 Scott Aaronson wrote that the ω = 9/4 lower bound and a matching Fourier-transform bound (N(log N)^{1/2+o(1)}) are a “whole new continent of mathematical truth”, that he now assumes lab proofs are correct “barring information to the contrary”, and that he hears from multiple sources that labs hold unreleased cryptography “bombshells” (unverified; see Mathematics). The oai-math-revised hub merged PR #82 on November 26, linking an outside Lean formalisation of the “Nearly quartic separation” manuscript. Still no new withdrawals, no outside review of the November 24 families, and no ETH review-blog post since November 12.
background: What it is: On October 6, 2026, OpenAI published "Sharing AI progress in mathematics" and a GitHub repository (github.com/openai/math). It holds 722 manuscripts in 372 result families, produced by an unreleased internal model that was tried on about 4,000 problems and averaged roughly three hours per result. The release was coordinated with the IAS-hosted Advisory Group on Mathematics and AI (members include Terence Tao, Timothy Gowers, Martin Hairer and Edward Witten).

Note: could not verify a single "~700-page" OpenAI paper. The story that matches is this release of 700+ papers, whose longest documents run to a few hundred pages: the 7/8 quasi-Riemann manuscript is 199 pages, and the Navier–Stokes paper is reportedly 166 pages (unconfirmed). The manuscripts list no individual human authors.

Contested: Tao (The Observer) and Buckmaster (on Tao's blog) both describe a roughly 10,000-agent effort on Navier–Stokes; OpenAI disputes Tao's account of the spending and the suspended sign-ups, and the "three hours per result" figure is said by Buckmaster to exclude failed attempts. None of this could be independently verified. A separate citation analysis by Hüseyin Uğur Yıldız finds 390 of the 722 manuscripts cite at least one OpenAI-authored work. On the Cheeky Pint podcast (October 29), Sam Altman himself estimated that OpenAI had spent "in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars" on mathematical problems, including around $10 million, "maybe a little more", on Navier–Stokes (as reported by The Verge). This could not be independently verified.

October 26 claims: OpenAI says the ETH disproof was found October 16 and formalised the next day, and the local smoothing proof was generated October 18 and formalised a day later. The October 26 changelog gives no updated formalisation total (it was 300/719, about 42%, on October 7).

ETH, two claims: OpenAI and Anthropic each say an internal model refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis on October 16; the commits landed about six hours apart on October 26 (Eastern). Anthropic's bound is 2^O(n log log n/√log n), checked by Comparator and the independent nanoda kernel. Anthropic's Levent Alpöge suggested that OpenAI had built on existing work. No Lean-checked details of OpenAI's runtime beyond its changelog wording could be verified. Since then, Kintali and O'Donnell have published simpler human-readable versions; O'Donnell's bound is one log log n factor weaker than OpenAI's. Fortnow notes the result does not help with Subset Sum or the Travelling Salesman problem.

New estimate, not verified: the UK Academy for the Mathematical Sciences' October 28 report estimates the forced Navier–Stokes run at about 10,000 agents, 88 hours and 130 billion output tokens (about £5 million at list prices), and counts 719 manuscripts, 300 of them formalised. These are the authors' estimates; OpenAI has not published compute figures.

New, not verified: at ADIPEC on November 2, Altman said the Navier–Stokes model is "the next GPT", "going to be released soon", run as 10,000 agents for about four days. This matches the ~10,000-agent accounts from Tao, Buckmaster and the AcadMathSci report. The quote comes from the event video as relayed on X; no mainstream transcript was found. The New Yorker (November 1) reports Buckmaster's account that OpenAI's Sébastien Bubeck offered him authorship of the Navier–Stokes paper if he excluded Alpöge. That is his account, not verified. The New Yorker also counts "an initial group of twenty-five Fields medallists" on the September open letter, against 28 signatories in other reports (probably the later total).

Human re-derivations keep arriving. Lei and Ren's two-part exposition of OpenAI's Navier–Stokes finite-time blowup with smooth forcing (Part I, arXiv 2609.35406; Part II, arXiv 2611.06869, 105 pages) claims no new mathematics and aims to make the proof readable. It is not a verdict on whether the proof is correct. Cárdenes Wuttig and Tindall's MUB paper (arXiv 2611.06917) reaches OpenAI's dimension-six result by a different route, through the connectedness of order-six complex Hadamard matrices and an interval-arithmetic covering. It is the first full classification in a non-prime-power dimension.

Unverified: the ETH review group's comment threads now include many self-described AI-produced or AI-assisted claims. Among them: Gheorghiu–Gupte quantum-circuit sampling (with ChatGPT Astra); Weitnauer's noncommutative circuit bounds (Codex and Claude); Toledo's Lean bridges, which take Anthropic's machine model, and OpenAI's via Daniel Hawkley's bridge theorems, to cslib's multitape Turing machine; and Yann Tal's (Tel Aviv) claim, produced with "ChatGPT 6 Pro", that the Wilson quotient mod p can be computed in time 2^O(log p/√log log p) using OpenAI's tensor-contraction theorem. None has been refereed. There is also one off-topic "Relational Geometry Program" request for review.

The Moshkovitz talk "The Unique Games Conjecture – Proved (!!?)" took place at UT Austin on November 4. According to Aaronson, it was a three-hour public lecture with "nearly 200 people" in person or on Zoom, based on her joint study of OpenAI's proof with Khot, Håstad and Minzer. The video will be posted "as soon as we can manage it". No account of what she concluded had been published as of November 6.

Caveat on reuse: TCSExam (Moonshot AI/Tsinghua, November 5) found that agents with internet access fetched OpenAI's published Ryser and MIRUP counterexamples and adapted them to the benchmark. Benchmarks of open problems may now be contaminated by the release. Separately, Dan Margalit told Axios (November 4) that "a number" of the released papers face retraction; the public changelog still records only the three October 7 withdrawals.

New context (November 6–8): outside OpenAI's release, AI-found results keep landing. Physical Superintelligence announced a Lean-checked proof of the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture found by a system running a non-public Anthropic model, and Aaronson says he believes it. Hofscheier and Nill's counterexamples are among the first published results to state openly that the model built on one of OpenAI's released manuscripts.

Review friction (November 9): the oai-math-revised hub is now arguing over what it can accept. Its maintainers reverted a 94,000-line Lean contribution for the BFSS manuscript because no one could realistically review it, while keeping smaller, checkable notes. The episode shows the same verification bottleneck that OpenAI's release created, now one level down.

New context (November 16): Turing Agent’s claim of completing three previously unformalised OpenAI TCS results is the authors’ own; the Lean code and whether it matches OpenAI’s original statements have not been independently checked here. Semantic review in the paper used GPT-6.1 Sol as a judge.

New context (November 21–22): the verification statement is from the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative as quoted by The Guardian and The Decoder; their own statement and Andrew Sutherland’s list of independent checks were not read directly here. The Decoder calls Alpöge a Stanford mathematician; The Guardian and his earlier essay describe him as working at Anthropic.

New (November 23–24): OpenAI’s VP ≠ VNP manuscript is item 379 in CONTENTS.md. Its Lean Comparator challenge states exact VP ≠ VNP over every field with the three standard axioms; the Lean documentation says the stronger border-circuit bound exp(Ω((log n)^(5/4))) is proved only in the paper. The files do not say whether anyone at OpenAI checked the proof. Anthropic’s competing 70-page paper states that no human mathematician has checked it. Which lab found the result first cannot be verified: OpenAI dates its result November 6, but Anthropic published first.

New (November 24–25): the nine manuscripts form families 379 (“Euclidean tensor geometry and its applications to complexity and combinatorics”, seven papers) and 380 (“Strongly polynomial-time linear programming”, two papers). The matrix-multiplication paper states its lower bound for formal arithmetic circuits (at least n^(9/4)/2 multiplication or division gates) and says the upper bound “was known”; Crypto Briefing’s claim of an earlier October 2 OpenAI preprint with that upper bound could not be verified here. The Lean documentation for family 380 covers strongly polynomial LP over rational data, not the paper’s real-coefficient claim, and the infinite-dimensional part of the tensor geometry is unformalised. Reactions so far come from blogs (Viola, Aaronson, Fortnow) and secondary sites (MLQ.ai, Crypto Briefing); no expert has publicly checked the new proofs.

New (November 25–26): Aaronson’s post refers to OpenAI and Anthropic “uploading more files” overnight, but the only repository changes found are OpenAI’s November 24 commit (merged 00:18 UTC November 25) and Anthropic’s VP ≠ VNP commit of November 23. His crypto claim is explicitly second-hand; treat as rumour. The outside formalisation linked in oai-math-revised PR #82 (wcook04/quartic-query-lean) states Theorem 1.1 with no hypotheses, according to the PR text; not independently checked.

dossiers.title: Astra vs. the answer key: when the model was right and the experts were wrong
dossiers.update: No change to TheoPhysEval: version 2 (November 12) is still the latest, it still does not list which expert keys were wrong, and Astra’s corrected score remains 49/50. Related today: the independent Yang–Mills group published its assessment of OpenAI’s November 4 Yang–Mills release, which matches perturbation theory at every finite order but still proves no mass gap (see Physics); the group’s October assessment said Astra was used to digest the Lean code. On ShellBench, GPT-6 Astra tops 100 everyday agent tasks at 62.5% (see Benchmarks).
background: The specifics: Astra is OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, announced in early September 2026. The "study" is the TheoPhysEval benchmark paper (arXiv 2610.16733), by 35 researchers from ICTS Bengaluru, Harvard, KU Leuven, Google DeepMind and other institutions, coordinated by Suvrat Raju. Running in OpenAI's Codex with web search, Astra scored 49/50 on the realistic track and 46/50 on the isolated track, against 46/50 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 34 for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Wherever the experts' keys turned out to be wrong, Astra's answer was correct. One problem (A.1.2) defeated every model. The realistic-track run cost USD 116.28, about USD 2.33 per problem.

Could not verify which specific problems were affected or the exact score before correction. A Chinese repost claims an initial score of about 88% and quotes a researcher who is not on the author list; the paper gives no such figure, so the claim is not used here.

Context, from November 3–5: the chiral-fermion thread now runs from Craig (arXiv 2610.09093, October 6, Astra “essential”) to Hsu (arXiv 2610.29019, October 21, appendix “mostly GPT Astra”) to Witten (arXiv 2611.05051, November 3, Claude-assisted). Witten concludes the approach is implementable in principle but not by Monte Carlo, since the chiral fermion path integral is not positive. Peter Woit (November 4) welcomed Witten's note and its credit to Claude Opus 5.5, and says he has new ideas of his own on the problem.

A MindStudio blog post (November 3) and a Neoteo explainer (October 26) retell the TheoPhysEval story and add nothing new. Secondary blogs again repeat the unsourced ~88% initial-score figure, which the paper does not give.

Update on the 'hairer/humanise-yang-mills' repository (created November 10): it now pins OpenAI’s released source (commit 3456e5e) and coordinates agent-assisted contributors to write a human-readable monograph. The account owner’s identity is still not independently confirmed.

New context (November 15–16): Craig’s chiral-fermion preprint was already in this timeline (October 6, Astra described as “essential”). The new OpenAI science-blog post is Craig’s first detailed account of the division of labour. Outlets covering it (The Defiant, RuntimeWire, aiweekly) differ on framing — “open for more than 50 years” versus a challenge dating to Lüscher’s 1998 work — and the OpenAI post itself could not be read directly (openai.com blocks automated access), so details come from secondary reports. The outside review by Golterman, Kronfeld and Shamir is Craig’s description, not their endorsement.

New context (November 16–17): The Decoder piece contains a claim that the Clay Institute said Navier–Stokes had “apparently been settled”; that has not been confirmed from a primary source and is not repeated here.
